idiom_name: policy-based authorization: [Authorize(Policy=...)] / RequireAuthorization plus IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync for point-of-use checks
implementation_notes: ASP.NET Core supplies the always-invoked property for the request edge: the authorization middleware evaluates an endpoint's policies on every request, and RequireAuthorization(...) or [Authorize(Policy = "...")] attach them declaratively, so the failure mode to test for is the endpoint that never got one. For object-level access the framework's resource-based authorization is the realization of the point-of-use rule: IAuthorizationService.AuthorizeAsync(user, resource, policy) runs after the resource has been loaded, because the earlier pipeline check could not see it - that is where per-object decisions belong. The classic in-process mechanism (Code Access Security and its Demand) has been retired from .NET, so complete mediation today is the framework's middleware, an explicit mediator class wrapping the resource, or a central decision service that both call; a mediator class is what you write when the object is not reached through a request.
pitfalls: Minimal-API endpoints without RequireAuthorization (or with AllowAnonymous) are anonymous by default, so the middleware never runs for them - the completeness claim has to be tested endpoint by endpoint.
Storing an AuthorizationResult or policy outcome in a singleton or long-lived scoped service outlives the request, so a cached decision survives revocation.
Checking the wrong instance (a DTO or an unloaded entity instead of the resource that will be served) is the framework-level equivalent of check-then-use.
A custom IAuthorizationHandler that calls context.Succeed(...) on a code path it does not really evaluate turns the mediator into a rubber stamp; handlers must fail closed.
